question: Does initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention reduce net cardiovascular harm in adults aged 60 and over?

framing.restatement: In adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, does starting low-dose aspirin, compared with not starting it, reduce cardiovascular events enough to outweigh treatment-related harms?
scope_in: Initiation of low-dose aspirin, generally 75–100 mg daily, versus no initiation or placebo.
Adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Prevention of first myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death.
Treatment-related harms, particularly intracranial hemorrhage and major extracranial bleeding.
Absolute and relative effects over specified follow-up periods, including differences by age, baseline cardiovascular risk, and bleeding risk.
Net effects under explicit outcome definitions and benefit–harm weighting.
scope_out: Secondary prevention in people with established cardiovascular disease.
Whether people already taking aspirin should discontinue it.
Higher-dose aspirin or aspirin prescribed for other indications.
Cancer prevention as a separate reason to initiate aspirin.
Individual prescribing decisions without information about the person's cardiovascular and bleeding risks.
presuppositions: Primary prevention denotes treatment in people without established cardiovascular disease.
Low-dose aspirin initiation and the comparison strategy can be specified sufficiently to distinguish their effects.
Net cardiovascular harm can be operationalized using an explicit set of cardiovascular outcomes and treatment-related harms.
A follow-up period and a method for comparing outcomes of different severity can be specified; different choices may yield different net effects.
Adults aged 60 and older may have heterogeneous effects, so a single conclusion may require qualification by age and baseline risk.
framing.answerhood: A complete answer would state whether initiation increases, decreases, or does not clearly change net harm, and quantify the absolute magnitude over a specified time horizon. It would report cardiovascular benefits and bleeding harms separately, then combine them using an explicit endpoint or severity-weighting rule, avoiding double-counting overlapping outcomes. Comparisons would hold the target population, aspirin regimen, follow-up duration, and outcome definitions constant, with age- and risk-specific results where they materially change the conclusion.

claims.text: Among adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, initiating aspirin 75–100 mg daily reduces the five-year risk of a first occurrence of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular death, intracranial hemorrhage, or major extracranial bleeding by at least 1 event per 1,000 people compared with no initiation. This net-benefit definition weights each component equally and counts each person only once.
claims.rationale: Prevented ischemic events could outnumber additional major bleeding events under an explicitly unweighted endpoint.

claims.text: Among adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, initiating aspirin 75–100 mg daily increases the five-year risk of a first occurrence of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular death, intracranial hemorrhage, or major extracranial bleeding by at least 1 event per 1,000 people compared with no initiation. This net-harm definition weights each component equally and counts each person only once.
claims.rationale: Additional major bleeding events could outnumber prevented ischemic events, particularly at older ages.

claims.text: Among adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, initiating aspirin 75–100 mg daily changes the five-year risk of the equally weighted, first-occurrence composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular death, intracranial hemorrhage, and major extracranial bleeding by less than 1 event per 1,000 people in either direction compared with no initiation.
claims.rationale: Cardiovascular benefits and major bleeding harms could approximately offset one another.

claims.text: An unweighted first-event composite of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular death, intracranial hemorrhage, and major extracranial bleeding measures the probability of experiencing at least one included event, but does not measure the total burden of fatality, disability, or recurrent events. Its component definitions must distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and count a fatal event only once.
claims.rationale: An equal-weight composite is a possible operationalization whose interpretation depends on event definitions and handling of overlap.

claims.text: A five-year quality-adjusted life-year endpoint can combine aspirin's cardiovascular benefits and bleeding harms by assigning each patient time in mutually exclusive health states after myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or major extracranial bleeding, with death assigned zero utility. This endpoint can yield a different benefit–harm conclusion from an equally weighted first-event composite because event severity, duration, and recurrence differ.
claims.rationale: A severity-weighted endpoint is a distinct operationalization that accommodates differences in consequences without adding overlapping event losses twice.

claims.text: Neither an equally weighted event composite nor a severity-weighted health-state measure can provide a coherent common endpoint for the cardiovascular and bleeding consequences of aspirin initiation.
claims.rationale: The proposed operationalizations require checking whether their components and accounting rules actually permit a coherent combined measure.

claims.text: The term 'net cardiovascular harm' does not identify a unique treatment effect: for the same population and follow-up, clinically plausible choices of included bleeding outcomes and severity weights can reverse whether aspirin initiation is classified as beneficial or harmful.
claims.rationale: The framing could conceal a consequential choice of endpoint rather than identify a single invariant net effect.

claims.rationale: Aspirin's antiplatelet action might not translate into prevention of these outcomes in this primary-prevention population.

claims.text: Among adults aged 60 years and older without established cardiovascular disease, initiating aspirin 75–100 mg daily increases five-year intracranial hemorrhage risk by 1–5 events per 1,000 people compared with no initiation, with a risk ratio between 1.20 and 1.70. definition.answer: A first-event composite classifies each patient by whether at least one included event occurs, rather than summing that patient's events or their severity. E40 explicitly defines a composite by first occurrence, and E45 describes time-to-first-event analysis. E13 and E21 document a distinct approach that explicitly assigns unequal mortality-based weights; those weights are not inherent in an unweighted first-event endpoint.

satisfies.answer: The endpoint proposed in C4 meets the first-event definition if it records each patient's earliest occurrence among the specified cardiovascular and bleeding events. Counting that union once per patient measures occurrence, not recurrent-event burden, disability, or severity-weighted fatality. Harmonization is necessary: E6 documents substitution of unspecified strokes for ischemic strokes; E54 shows that major hemorrhage already includes intracranial bleeding; and E44 and E81 show that serious bleeding can itself be fatal or disabling. Thus ischemic and hemorrhagic events must be distinguished, overlapping bleeding categories cannot be added as independent events, and a fatal event must not be counted again as both an event and a death. These records support the endpoint's conceptual interpretation and safeguards, not an observed estimate of the proposed combined endpoint.

arguments.note: This is a definitional argument for C4, not an inference about aspirin's treatment effect. The cited studies' separate cardiovascular and bleeding endpoints do not supply the patient-level union required to estimate this composite.

definition.answer: A first-event composite records whether a patient experiences at least one included event, using the earliest qualifying occurrence, rather than summing recurrent events or weighting their consequences. E40 explicitly defines a composite by first occurrence, and E45 describes time-to-first-event analysis. Unequal severity weights are an additional analytic choice, as illustrated by the mortality-weighted method in E13 and E21; they are not inherent in an unweighted composite.

satisfies.answer: The proposed endpoint satisfies this definition when each patient contributes only their earliest event from the specified union of cardiovascular and bleeding outcomes. Its interpretation is therefore occurrence of any included event, not total fatality, disability, or recurrent-event burden. The evidence establishes why component reconciliation matters: E6 documents substitution of unspecified strokes for ischemic strokes; E99 and E104 distinguish hemorrhagic from ischemic stroke; E105 explicitly includes hemorrhagic stroke within all intracranial bleeding; and E54 includes intracranial bleeding within major hemorrhage. These nested categories must not be added as independent events. E104 defines fatal events as events followed by death within 30 days, and E105 reports fatal cases as a subset of intracranial bleeding, supporting counting the qualifying fatal occurrence once rather than again as a separate death. E44 and E81 also show that bleeding definitions can include fatal or disabling events. Finally, E108 reports different observed case-fatality proportions for hemorrhagic and ischemic strokes, illustrating severity information that an equally weighted occurrence indicator does not encode.

arguments.note: This extends the existing definitional argument with explicit evidence about nested hemorrhage categories, fatal-event subsets, and unequal observed stroke severity. It does not infer an aspirin treatment effect from pooled case fatality, establish a five-year combined risk, or validate a QALY model.

conclusion.answer: The evidence gathered does not settle whether starting low-dose aspirin reduces, increases, or changes by less than 1 per 1,000 the five-year net risk in all adults aged 60 and older without cardiovascular disease (C1–C3 remain undecided). It leans against a net benefit, particularly in the predominantly age-70-and-older ASPREE population: over median follow-up of 4.7 years, cardiovascular-event rates were 10.7 versus 11.3 per 1,000 person-years with aspirin versus placebo, while major-hemorrhage rates were 8.6 versus 6.2. However, these separate outcomes have different definitions from the requested combined endpoint and cannot simply be subtracted to obtain a deduplicated five-year net effect (C4). Thus, a defensible absolute net magnitude for the full target population cannot be reported from this inquiry.

judgements.text: Neither net benefit, net harm, nor equivalence within 1 event per 1,000 over five years is established for the specified population and endpoint, because the retrieved estimates do not supply the aligned patient-level first-event union needed to distinguish those alternatives (C1–C3).

judgements.text: The direction of the retrieved ASPREE results leans against net benefit—its cardiovascular estimate was uncertain while major hemorrhage increased—but this does not establish the specified five-year net-harm threshold (C1, C2).
judgements.rests_on: E3 reports a cardiovascular-event HR of 0.95 (95% CI 0.83–1.08), and E4 reports a major-hemorrhage HR of 1.38 (1.18–1.62), in a predominantly age-70-and-older population with separate endpoints.

judgements.text: An equally weighted first-event composite measures whether a person experiences any included event, not total mortality, disability, or recurrent-event burden, and must distinguish stroke types and count overlapping or fatal events only once (C4).
judgements.rests_on: The first-occurrence definition in E40, nested bleeding categories in E54 and E105, and the independently described ASCEND safety endpoint in E81 underpin the accepted classification in A1–A2.

what_would_change_this: A randomized comparison in adults aged 60 and older receiving 75–100 mg daily, reporting five-year cumulative risks and uncertainty for the exact deduplicated first-event composite, would distinguish C1–C3 if its risk-difference interval supported a reduction of at least 1 per 1,000, an increase of at least 1 per 1,000, or a change strictly within those bounds.

Aligned five-year component results, including fatal bleeding separately, with results for ages 60–69 versus 70 or older and baseline cardiovascular and bleeding risks, would resolve the component and subgroup claims C8–C15.

A specified five-year health-state analysis with explicit utilities, recurrence handling, and results alongside the unweighted composite in the same population would address C5; a demonstrated reversal under plausible alternative weights would address the weighting concern in C7.

An implemented endpoint that sums recurrent events, assigns severity weights, or counts fatal and overlapping events more than once would require changing its interpretation from the first-event occurrence measure accepted in C4.
unresolved: The direction and absolute magnitude of the five-year net effect for the full age-60-and-older population remain unresolved (C1–C3).
Exact five-year cardiovascular component effects, bleeding component effects, fatal-event effects, and age- and risk-specific treatment differences remain unresolved (C8–C15).

The proposed five-year QALY construction and whether plausible severity weights reverse the benefit–harm conclusion remain unresolved (C5 and C7); the retrieved lifetime modeling does not settle those questions.

Repeated publications from ASPREE or ASCEND and the overlapping arguments A1–A2 must not be treated as independent treatment-effect corroboration.

candidates.title: Preclinical Alzheimer's disease: Definition, natural history, and diagnostic criteria.
candidates.snippet: During the past decade, a conceptual shift occurred in the field of Alzheimer's disease (AD) considering the disease as a continuum. Thanks to evolving biomarker research and substantial discoveries, it is now possible to identify the disease even at the preclinical stage before the occurrence of the first clinical symptoms. This preclinical stage of AD has become a major research focus as the field postulates that early intervention may offer the best chance of therapeutic success. To date, very little evidence is established on this "silent" stage of the disease. A clarification is needed about the definitions and lexicon, the limits, the natural history, the markers of progression, and the ethical consequence of detecting the disease at this asymptomatic stage. This article is aimed at addressing all the different issues by providing for each of them an updated review of the literature and evidence, with practical recommendations.

candidates.title: Epidemiology and causes of preterm birth.
candidates.snippet: This paper is the first in a three-part series on preterm birth, which is the leading cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality in developed countries. Infants are born preterm at less than 37 weeks' gestational age after: (1) spontaneous labour with intact membranes, (2) preterm premature rupture of the membranes (PPROM), and (3) labour induction or caesarean delivery for maternal or fetal indications. The frequency of preterm births is about 12-13% in the USA and 5-9% in many other developed countries; however, the rate of preterm birth has increased in many locations, predominantly because of increasing indicated preterm births and preterm delivery of artificially conceived multiple pregnancies. Common reasons for indicated preterm births include pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, and intrauterine growth restriction. Births that follow spontaneous preterm labour and PPROM-together called spontaneous preterm births-are regarded as a syndrome resulting from multiple causes, including infection or inflammation, vascular disease, and uterine overdistension. Risk factors for spontaneous preterm births include a previous preterm birth, black race, periodontal disease, and low maternal body-mass index. A short cervical length and a raised cervical-vaginal fetal fibronectin concentration are the strongest predictors of spontaneous preterm birth.
